title: The Heart in your day
hookLine: Zen, Tibetan, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities chant it daily

lines: A WOODEN DRUM SHAPED LIKE A FISH.
cards: Before sunrise at a Zen monastery in Japan, someone strikes a wooden drum shaped like a fish, and the monks start chanting at a steady, rolling clip. In a Korean temple, the same text, a different sound.
In a Tibetan monastery, a longer version that opens on a mountain with the Buddha in meditation. In Vietnamese and Chinese temples from Taipei to Toronto, the same words at the morning service.
For ten days you've read it one line at a time. People who chant it daily often know it by heart and get through it in a couple of minutes.

teach.b: The Heart Sutra is short enough to live with: one page. That's part of why it travels.
In Japan, people copy it out by hand with a brush, character by character, a practice called shakyō, and temples collect the copies. It shows up on fans, on tea bowls, on scrolls in family altars.

Tibetan Buddhists chant a longer version with a frame story: the Buddha sits in deep meditation on Vulture Peak while Avalokiteshvara and Shariputra talk, and at the end the Buddha comes out and says, well done.
The name carries a double meaning.
Hṛdaya in Sanskrit means heart, and also core, the essence.
This is the heart of the huge Perfection of Wisdom literature, squeezed into one page. Now put the ten days back together. Prajnaparamita: wisdom gone beyond.
Avalokiteshvara looked deep and saw the heaps were empty.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form: nothing stands alone. Emptiness is not nothing; the cup still holds tea. Not born, not destroyed.
No eye, no ear: hold lists lightly. Nothing to attain. No walls, so no fear.

And the mantra, gone beyond. If one line has to go with you, let it be the one this whole part turns on: form is emptiness. The chair, the phone, your own hands: real, useful, and made entirely of other things.

how: Zen, Tibetan, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhist communities chant the Heart Sutra in daily services, often to the beat of a wooden fish drum, and in Japan many people copy it by hand as a practice called shakyō.

o: the life breath that keeps a body going
love, the warm feeling you have for others
heart, and also core: the essence of something

games.q: match each line of the Heart Sutra to what it meant.

games.q: a friend in Japan wants a slow, quiet way to spend an afternoon with the Heart Sutra. what practice does today's lesson describe?

reading a summary of it online.
games.why: shakyō, hand-copying sutras with a brush, is a common practice in Japan, and temples collect the copies.

practice: If you have a copy of the Heart Sutra nearby, read it through once, slowly, aloud or silently, the way temples chant it at their morning services.

If you don't, sit with its most well-known line: on the in-breath, form is emptiness; on the out-breath, emptiness is form. Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object, a mug, a window, and see it as both.

wordCard.voice: Hṛdaya. Heart, and also core or essence in Sanskrit: the name for this one-page sutra, chanted daily across Asia and beyond.

orig.note: Sanskrit hṛdaya: heart, and also core or essence; the sutra's full name is Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya.

carryVoice: Your line: form is emptiness. Ten days, one page, one line to keep. Until tomorrow.
